summary: Antje B. Weaver generally supports the Draft Environmental Statement as sound and in the interest of all public lands users, while acknowledging that some environmental damage is unavoidable. She takes issue with specific claims in the draft, such as the assertion that ORVs strengthen family ties, and questions why rallies and races should be permitted on public lands when existing facilities could be used instead. She also expresses doubt that the proposal will be effectively implemented given budget cuts to federal agencies.

statement.text:
Director, Bureau of Outdoor Recreation Department of the Interior C Street between 18th and 19th, N. W. Washington, D. C. 20240
Dear Mr. Watt:
I read with great interest the Draft Enviornmental Statement of the proposed implementation of Executive Order 11644 pertaining to use of off-road vehicles on the Public lands prepared by your Bureau on May 26, 1972.
On the whole, the proposal is sound and in the interest of all users of public lands. It is evident that, given our society and our standards, some long term damage to the environment cannot be avoided. But we should try to minimize the damage.
I have the following comments:
1. On page 12 of the Draft Enviornmental Statement I take issue with the statement that "ORV's can strengthen family ties." That may be so, but I don't think the use of these vehicles should be promoted on that basis, since there are numerous ways of strengthening family ties which do not pollute the air with fumes and noise and damage the enviornment physically.
2. In part b, Operating Criteria, page 6, it is stated that permits may granted for rallies, contests and organized races on land approved for such purposes. Why should there be such activities at all on public lands? Why can't these be held at facilities already existing for drag racing, stock-car racing and demolition derbies? Many communities have these facilities already--by using them the ORV users would not cause any damage at all, probably save a great deal of money and be close to help in case of accident.
3. Any program, to be effectively executed, must have sufficient manpower and funds. In view of the fact that President Nixon has made significant cuts in the budgets of many Federal agencies, I am doubtful that your proposal will be very effective, unless you are able to obtain trained manpower and funds for the implementation of your Draft Enviornmental Statement. After all, a program is only as good as the people who execute it, and in this case you need many and good people to do a good job.
Thank you for the opportunity to make these comments.
Very truly yours,
111
Antje B. Weaver
